claims.text: A predominantly first-row transition-metal dendritic high-entropy alloy containing less than 10% platinum-group metals will improve catalytic activity and durability under automotive exhaust conditions.
The proposed catalyst will reduce PGM loading by approximately 70% relative to conventional automotive catalysts.
A PS-PVP-PEO block-copolymer-mediated one-pot solvothermal reduction in DMF can produce dendritic high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The block-copolymer architecture and reducing environment of DMF promote confined nucleation, simultaneous coreduction, and compositionally uniform alloying.
The synthesis will preserve atomic-scale mixing when adapted from five noble metals to a first-row transition-metal matrix containing trace PGMs.
The resulting nanoparticles will have a defect-rich, high-surface-area architecture.
Trace PGMs will be well dispersed and optimally positioned within the non-PGM high-entropy matrix.
Atomic-scale mixing will induce synergistic electronic effects between first-row transition metals and trace PGMs.
The synergistic effects will optimize adsorption energies of reactants and reaction intermediates.
The proposed alloy structure will promote oxygen-vacancy formation.
Optimized adsorption and increased oxygen-vacancy formation will enhance CO and NOx conversion.
The dendritic high-entropy structure will mitigate nanoparticle sintering and catalyst deactivation.
The proposed catalyst will have a lower light-off temperature than a commercial high-PGM automotive catalyst.
The proposed catalyst will have higher turnover frequencies for CO and NOx conversion than the high-PGM baseline.
The proposed catalyst will maintain comparable or improved activity during prolonged redox cycling.
Standard high-PGM automotive catalysts typically have higher light-off temperatures and deactivate faster under redox cycling.
The predicted improvement should hold from 300 to 600 °C in CO-, NOx-, and hydrocarbon-containing simulated exhaust if dendritic morphology and atomic-scale mixing are maintained.
Loss of synthesis control during scale-up could compromise morphology, mixing, and catalytic performance.
